Milwaukee, WI Property Tax Guide: Offices, Dates and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Wisconsin

  • Milwaukee, WI Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Behind on Milwaukee property tax?

Who bills and collects the tax

City Hall houses both offices you'll deal with. Upstairs in Room 507 (200 E. Wells Street) the Assessor decides what each parcel is worth, at 414-286-3651. Down in Room 103 the City Treasurer mails the bill and takes your money, at 414-286-2240.

Milwaukee is the county seat, yet you pay the city treasurer, not a county office, since the city collects its own taxes. The bill is a combined one, and special charges or assessments can be added. Any that remain unpaid in mid-November may be rolled into the property tax bill, collected as a tax, and can't be appealed, negotiated or compromised.

An estimated 562,407 people lived in Milwaukee on July 1, 2025, a drop of 2.7 percent from April 2020. Owners occupy just 41.8 percent of housing units. Median value of an owner-occupied home: $184,000. Median gross rent: $1,059. Households: 232,520.

Due dates and ways to pay

January 31 is the deadline for the full bill or for the first installment. By default, Wis. Stat. 74.11 splits the tax into two equal halves, due January 31 and July 31, and a parcel whose total tax is below $100 must be settled in full by January 31. Milwaukee adds a longer plan, described below.

The treasurer accepts payment these ways:

  • Check by mail, in the reply envelope printed for your bill. No cash.
  • Drop box: the City Hall Market Street entrance box is available at any hour.
  • Phone (414-286-2240) or website: a card costs a 2.75 percent fee with a $3.00 floor, but a bank transfer by ACH from checking or savings costs nothing.
  • Your bank's bill-pay tool, addressed to City Treasurer, City Hall, Room 103, 200 East Wells Street, Milwaukee, WI 53202.

A letter dropped in a street mailbox may not be postmarked that day, so mail early or use a drop box. Tyler payments after 4:00 p.m. Central are credited on the next business day.

Installment plan

Can't cover the whole bill? The city spreads it over ten months with no interest, provided the bill is over $100 and the first payment is in by January 31. Tyler Auto Pay can pull each month's payment from a bank account or card automatically.

If you sell before the ten months are up, the treasurer can quote what remains, and the closing agent needs that number.

Key tax dates

StepWhen

Second installment (state default)July 31
Lottery credit claim at the treasurerJanuary 31 after the bill arrives
Late lottery credit claim to the stateOctober 1 after the bill is issued

The next Open Book period starts the fourth Monday in April 2027. Put that date and the January 31 payment deadline on your calendar, since both repeat every year and missing either one costs money or appeal rights.

How to appeal your assessment

Your written objection is due at the Assessor's Office on the third Monday in May. The city prefers the Milwaukee Real Property Appeals web application at milwaukee.gov/assessorobjection, open for new forms only during Open Book. Paper is fine too, mailed to 200 E Wells Street, Room 507, Milwaukee, WI 53202, or delivered weekdays between 8:00 a.m. and 4:45 p.m. An emailed form is treated as never filed.

You can send evidence after the form. The assessor accepts these for a house:

  • An appraisal that captures the market on January 1 of this year.
  • A comparable-sales analysis from a local agent, dated the same day.
  • Pictures of repairs put off, as they stood January 1.
  • Pictures proving something listed on your property record card didn't exist on January 1.

An appraiser studies your appeal, then the Board of Assessors rules and sends notice. Still unhappy? Request a Board of Review hearing through the clerk at boardreview@milwaukee.gov or 414-286-3742. Wis. Stat. 70.47 asks for advance notice of your intent at least 48 hours before the first meeting, followed by the written objection inside that meeting's opening two hours, though the board can excuse notice for good cause. Commercial owners who skip the income and expense statement (PR-323) may be barred from testifying before the Board of Review.

Late payments

Once a payment is missed, the tax is delinquent and interest accrues. Under Wis. Stat. 74.47, delinquent general property taxes and special charges bear one percent for each month or part of a month. Ordinance can add up to 0.5 percent monthly for a county board or a city authorized under s. 74.87, which is why the treasurer's payoff quote matters.

If the first installment hasn't arrived five working days past January 31, everything still owing is delinquent on February 1 (s. 74.11(7)). The interest-free city plan also hinges on that first payment.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Lottery credit and exemptions

The lottery and gaming credit is the main one for homeowners. To get it, live in the dwelling you own as your primary Wisconsin residence on January 1 of the levy year. Rental units, business property, vacant land and garages are out, and each owner gets one primary residence. Questions on city parcels go to the treasurer.

Credit absent from your bill? Apply to the treasurer by the next January 31, or make a late claim to the Department of Revenue by October 1. The credit belongs to the property, so count it when the tax is prorated between buyer and seller. Exempt owners find forms on the assessor's site, and requests are due March 1.

Selling with taxes owed

Find out the balance before saying yes to an offer. Bills appear in the treasurer's Resident Access system, and assessed values in the assessor's Real Property Search. Tax rates for every year since 1984 are posted too, if you want the trend.

Work through these points when you sell:

  • Request the precise balance from the treasurer, special charges from November included.
  • Check with the closing agent about how your contract divides the bill with the buyer.
  • Make sure the deed gets recorded; every permanent ownership or name change goes to the Milwaukee County Register of Deeds.
  • The buyer should file a mailing address change with the Assessor in Room 507, otherwise a refund might be mailed to you.

In a cash sale, back taxes are normally paid out of your proceeds at closing, so an unpaid balance needn't block the deal. Interest keeps accruing until payoff, so request a figure that holds through closing day.

Frequently asked questions

What is the deadline?

January 31 for the whole bill or a first installment, with July 31 as the state default for a second. Bills over $100 can alternatively go on the city's ten-month plan with no interest, if the first payment is in by January 31.

How do I pay?

Through the City Treasurer in City Hall Room 103 at 200 East Wells Street, by mailed check, drop box, phone or website. Cash can't be used.

When can I contest my value?

During Open Book, the fourth Monday in April through the third Monday in May. That last Monday is the yearly objection deadline, and filing goes to the Assessor's Office.

Can I sell owing tax?

Yes. Get a payoff quote from the treasurer first, since state law charges one percent a month on late tax, and the closing agent can settle it from your proceeds if the contract permits.

City or county?

The city, through its Treasurer. Deeds, and the state transfer fee, are handled by the County Register of Deeds.

Who sends the bill

Two city offices touch your bill. The Clerk/Treasurer mails it and collects the money. The City Assessor's Office sets the value it rests on. The Clerk/Treasurer department prepares the bills for property and business owners, takes in real estate taxes and keeps the Board of Review hearing record.

The Assessor's Office discovers, lists and values each taxable property in the city, and it levies nothing. Take a dollar-amount question to the taxing bodies. Take a question about the value on your property record to the assessor.

After July 31 the city passes its real estate tax records to the Waukesha County Treasurer, who collects every delinquent real estate tax. That office is at 515 W. Moreland Blvd., Room AC148, Waukesha, WI 53188, open weekdays 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. The phone is 262-548-7029.

The Waukesha tax rate

The net rate on the 2025 Waukesha tax bills is $13.42 per $1,000 of valuation: a gross rate of $14.46 less a state credit of $1.04. Four taxing bodies share the bill, and the city itself keeps a little over half.

Taxing jurisdictionLevyRate per $1,000Share of the tax dollar
City of Waukesha$79,645,364$7.7953.8%
Waukesha School District$52,377,618$5.1235.41%

Early each December the rates are set from the taxing bodies' levies, so the coming year's rate shows up on the bill that arrives this winter. Valuation times rate gives a rough bill.

Due dates and installments

The city offers three installments. Pay everything or the first third by January 31, the second by March 31 and the third by May 31. No further bills follow the first mailing, so keep the installment coupons that come with it.

Current real estate taxes are collected at the Clerk/Treasurer from mid-December through July 31. Due dates are printed on your bill, and 262-524-3850 reaches the office if you want to confirm them.

The three-date plan is unusual. The county's due date table shows January 31 and July 31 for most Waukesha County municipalities, including the separate Waukesha Village entry. Only the City of Waukesha, New Berlin and Sussex follow January 31, March 31 and May 31. Owners near the city line should check which municipality bills the parcel.

Ways to pay

Five ways to pay are listed by the city, and a lender can also pay from escrow:

  • Web: tax.waukeshacounty.gov accepts an eCheck for $1.50, a debit card for $3.95 or a credit card at 2.39 percent of the payment.
  • Bank: any Waukesha State Bank branch takes payment with the bill or stub, and you need not bank there.
  • Mail: Waukesha City Hall, Attn: Clerk/Treasurer Office, 201 Delafield Street, Waukesha, WI 53188, with the check payable to City of Waukesha.
  • Drop box: open around the clock at City Hall and at the Waukesha Public Library, 321 Wisconsin Avenue. Staff process what is left there the next business day.
  • Counter: first floor of City Hall, weekdays, 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

When your mortgage company pays the tax, ask when it will go out. An escrow check made out to both the city and the homeowner must be signed on the back by every person named, and an escrow overage refund can take four to six weeks by mail.

How does a Waukesha assessment appeal work?

The Waukesha Board of Review takes objections, and the city announces the filing deadline each spring. The yearly sequence: the assessor issues real estate notices, an open book period follows, objections are due at 9:00 a.m. shortly before the first hearing, and that hearing starts at 9:00 a.m. in the Council Chambers at City Hall.

The next assessment date is January 1, 2027, and the assessor's page offers an online Request for Property Review application for it. Under Wis. Stat. 70.32, the assessor values real property at the full value it could ordinarily bring at a private sale.

The assessor's website also provides a property record card for each parcel, showing assessed value, lot size, building details and tax history. Pull yours before listing, because a buyer's agent will look at the same record.

If a Waukesha tax bill goes unpaid

Unpaid tax turns delinquent and begins to carry interest and penalty. Installments only work when each one is paid on time, because a single miss makes the entire remaining balance delinquent (Wis. Stat. 74.11 and 74.12). The charge runs 1.5 percent a month, counted back to February 1, until paid.

A mailed payment is timely under Wis. Stat. 74.69(1) if it is properly addressed, postmarked before midnight on the last day to pay and received by the treasurer within five business days afterward. The only exception is postal delay or administrative error found by a county board committee.

Foreclosure auctions for tax-delinquent property are run by the county treasurer on WisconsinSurplus.com. Behind on tax? Call 262-548-7029 for the payoff before a sale step goes any further.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Taxes and paperwork before closing

Get the present tax balance from the Clerk/Treasurer or the county treasurer and pass it to your closing agent for the settlement statement. A search by address or parcel number at tax.waukeshacounty.gov shows whether a bill has been paid.

Two other Wisconsin rules apply around then. Selling a one to four unit home? The buyer is owed a finished real estate condition report no later than 10 days after the contract is accepted (Wis. Stat. 709.02 and 709.03), and the form has a section for taxes, special assessments and permits. A late report lets the buyer rescind within two business days after the 10 days end. A court-appointed fiduciary who never lived in the house need not provide one.

For a mortgage payoff, a lender must answer a written request within seven business days when the loan is on residential property, and may not describe the payoff amount as subject to change before the payoff date (Wis. Stat. 708.15). Ask early and match the good-through date to your closing date.

About the city

Waukesha sits on the Fox River about 15 miles west of Milwaukee. The city calls itself the seventh largest in Wisconsin, with close to 72,000 residents, and the manufacturing hub of Waukesha County. It covers 25.07 square miles, about 24.8 of it land.

Four taxing bodies share each bill here, so ask the Clerk/Treasurer for the figures on your exact parcel instead of relying on a general rate.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Waukesha property tax?

Until July 31, the city's Clerk/Treasurer handles it, whether online, at a Waukesha State Bank branch, by mail, in a City Hall or library drop box, or at the 201 Delafield Street counter. Past that date, balances still owing go to the county treasurer at 515 W. Moreland Blvd.

What is the Waukesha property tax rate?

$13.42 per $1,000 of valuation on the 2025 bills, net. Behind it sits a $14.46 gross rate from the city, school district, county and technical college, reduced by a $1.04 state credit. The city's own portion is $7.79 per $1,000.

Can I pay Waukesha property tax in installments?

Yes, three of them: January 31, March 31 and May 31. A missed installment makes the remaining balance delinquent, so pay on time or pay once in full.

Who hears a Waukesha property assessment appeal?

Waukesha's Board of Review, with its record kept by the Clerk/Treasurer. The assessment notice arrives each spring, and your objection must beat the deadline stated on it.

What happens to Waukesha taxes after July 31?

Unpaid real estate tax records move from the city to the Waukesha County Treasurer, and the county collects. Delinquent balances carry 1.5 percent per month, counted from February 1.

Kenosha, WI Property Tax Guide: Offices, Dates and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Wisconsin
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Kenosha, WI Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Kenosha, WI Property Tax Guide sale
  • Turn the Kenosha, WI Property Tax Guide offer down and you owe us nothing

Owe Kenosha Property Tax? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Kenosha houses as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Behind on Kenosha property tax?
We buy Kenosha houses as-is, and the title company pays unpaid tax from the proceeds.

City or county: who gets the check

For current-year tax, the City of Kenosha is the payee through July 31. Kenosha County takes over after that date. A payment on a city parcel that lands at the county early gets sent back. The county does accept city-parcel payments for earlier tax years and for balances still delinquent after July 31.

The county treasurer's downtown office is inside the city limits, at 1010 56th Street, Kenosha, WI 53140, phone 262-653-2542. It collects delinquent and prior-year tax on city parcels and runs the tax deed process on parcels that stay unpaid. Each year the treasurer also settles with the school districts, Gateway Technical College and the state revenue department, so a single Kenosha bill carries the levies of several governments.

Due dates and weekend rule

Owners here can pay in one lump or in three pieces, on January 31, April 30 and July 31. The pattern comes from Wis. Stat. 74.12, which requires any installment ordinance to collect the first piece by January 31, at least half of the total by April 30 and the rest by July 31.

InstallmentDue date for 2026 taxesIf it falls on a weekend
FirstJanuary 31, 2027 (Sunday)Five-working-day window ends Friday, February 5, 2027
SecondApril 30, 2027 (Friday)None needed
ThirdJuly 31, 2027 (Saturday)Window ends Friday, August 6, 2027

December is when bills should arrive, with the mailing deadline set by 74.09(5) at the month's third Monday. Call the city treasurer to confirm exactly what you owe on each date, because the second and third installments depend on what you paid earlier.

When an installment is late

A late installment accelerates the rest of the bill, and interest begins. Miss the first installment and all unpaid tax is delinquent on February 1 (74.12(7)). Miss a later one and the unpaid balance is delinquent the next month's first day (74.12(8)), with interest and penalty counted from the earlier February 1 under 74.12(10).

The interest rate is 1 percent monthly, and by ordinance a county can add as much as 0.5 percent more (74.47). Kenosha County quotes 18 percent a year in all. Late money paid through July 31 goes to the city treasurer; then the city hands its roll to the county by August 15 and the county collects what remains (74.12(10) and (12)).

City residents are told to phone the city treasurer up to July 31 and the County Treasurer afterward. For tax that stays unpaid, the county can arrange a plan clearing each delinquent year within 10 months. Three years of delinquency opens tax deed foreclosure, so a seller with back tax should settle well before that.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How the bill is figured

The formula starts with assessed value divided by 1,000, times the combined mill rate. Total taxes, less the lottery credit and the first dollar credit, give net property taxes, and special assessments and special charges are added to reach the bill. The county's Property & Taxes page lists current and past county mill rates.

Your bill shows the rate for your parcel and the amount owed to each taxing body, so compare those lines from year to year before assuming the city raised its share.

Wisconsin limits how quickly a local levy can grow, but a bill can still jump. A higher assessment, a new special assessment for a street, sewer or sidewalk, or a voter-approved referendum can each do it. Bills must list recent referendum amounts under 74.09(3)(db).

Appealing your assessment

Call the City Assessor's Office first. If the answer stands, the Board of Review is next. City boards sit in the council chamber or another spot the council chooses (70.47(1)), at some point in the 45 days after the fourth Monday of April. The clerk posts the meeting notice at least 15 days ahead, or 30 days ahead when the city is revaluing.

The rules for appearing are strict:

  • Give the board clerk notice, spoken or written, 48 or more hours before the board first meets.
  • Hand over a written objection on the board's form during the opening two hours of that session.
  • Object to land and buildings together. You cannot contest only one.
  • Let the assessor see the outside of the property if asked. Under 70.47(7)(aa), an owner who refuses a reasonable certified-mail request gives up the right to appear.

A ruling against you starts a 90-day clock from the decision notice for a court action by certiorari (70.47(13)). Reach out to the assessor early next spring to learn when open book is held.

Selling with tax due

Who owes what for the sale year is a matter for the purchase contract. Where it says nothing, Wis. Stat. 74.15 has the seller repay the buyer for the months before closing, at one-twelfth of last year's tax per month, with the closing month counted when the deed is dated after the 15th. Many Kenosha contracts write their own proration, and in that case the title company's figure controls.

A seller who owes tax should ask the city treasurer, or the County Treasurer after July 31, for a payoff good through closing day. It includes interest and penalty, and an unpaid special assessment or special charge can put the whole parcel into delinquency. A mortgage escrow does not change this, since the owner is still responsible for making sure the lender paid. With a cash buyer the payoff is simply deducted at the closing table.

Some owners also get relief. The Lottery and Gaming Credit is for owners whose primary residence was the home on January 1. The Homestead Credit, claimed with state income tax, helps lower-income owners. Disabled service members can ask the County service office about the state's property tax credit for them.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Kenosha at a glance

The city lies on Lake Michigan's southwestern shore, roughly 32 miles south of Milwaukee and 49 miles north of Chicago. At 99,986 people in 2020 it ranked fourth among Wisconsin cities, and the 2025 estimate is 99,239. Metra commuter rail runs to Chicago, and I-94, WIS 50 and WIS 32 are the main roads.

The city has about 40,333 households. Owners live in 58.7 percent of homes, the median home value is $225,200, rent runs a median $1,186 and household income a median $71,239. The former AMC lakefront plant site is now the HarborPark neighborhood, and locals divide the city into Downtown, Uptown and the area west of I-94. Winters can be hard on roofs and gutters, so buyers often ask about their condition.

Frequently asked questions

When are Kenosha, WI property taxes due?

Either all at once or in three installments, January 31, April 30 and July 31. Current-year payments go to the City of Kenosha until July 31, then to the County Treasurer.

Do I pay Kenosha property tax to the city or the county?

Pay the City of Kenosha for current-year tax through July 31. Pay the Kenosha County Treasurer for prior-year tax and for delinquent balances after July 31.

How much interest is charged on late Kenosha property tax?

The rate is 1 percent monthly under Wis. Stat. 74.47, and the county lists interest and penalty together as 18 percent yearly, beginning February 1 after a missed first installment.

Can I sell my Kenosha house if I owe back property tax?

Yes. Ask the treasurer for a payoff figure valid through closing, and the balance gets cleared then. Paying sooner keeps you away from the tax deed process, which starts after three years of delinquency.

How do I contest my Kenosha property assessment?

Speak to the City Assessor's Office. Next, warn the Board of Review clerk 48 hours before the first meeting and file the objection inside its first two hours. Certiorari review in court has to start within 90 days of the decision notice.

Who assesses and who collects in Racine

Racine splits the work between two governments. The City Assessor Division sets your assessed value. The city itself takes tax payments through July 31, and the Racine County Treasurer collects whatever is still unpaid after that date. The city sits on Lake Michigan at the Root River mouth, 22 miles south of Milwaukee and 60 miles north of Chicago, and had 77,816 residents in the 2020 census. ZIP codes run from 53401 to 53408.

The Assessor Division works from City Hall, 730 Washington Avenue, Room 308. It holds the parcel legal descriptions, ownership records, property and sales data, and the assessment rolls. Questions can start at cityofracinewi.gov. For looking up what a given parcel owes, the county's Ascent Land Records tax search is the tool most owners use.

Due dates

Racine owners may pay in four parts. Every one of the four goes to the city, and bills are mailed in December. City payment questions go to (262) 636-9171.

Racine installment schedule
Due dateWhere to pay
January 31City of Racine
March 31City of Racine

Most of the rest of the county has two dates, not four. If you close in spring, you may be selling a house with two city payments still open, so settle who pays them in the contract.

Late or short payments

Miss a date, or pay less than the amount due, and the whole balance for the year comes due together. The four-part option ends. Interest and penalties begin February 1 under Wis. Stat. ss. 74.11(7) and 74.12(7), at a combined 1.5 percent per month under s. 74.47. The county treasurer has no room to adjust those charges.

  • Even a small shortfall on one installment has the same effect as skipping it.
  • After July 31 the leftover balance is payable to the county treasurer instead of the city.
  • The county invites owners with back taxes to arrange regular payments and takes them.

Before a sale closes, ask both offices for a year-by-year figure. The current year can be open with the city while an older year sits with the county.

How Racine values a house

State law requires assessment at market value. The Assessor Division defines that as the price a typical, well-informed buyer would pay with no pressure on either side. The assessor reads the market and does not invent a value. A revaluation is a full review of all assessments so they stay even across the city.

The division names the changes that usually push a value up: extra rooms or a garage, new siding, a substantially updated kitchen or bath, central air and extensive remodeling. Law calls for valuing from an actual view or the best information available, and the division says seeing inside and out works best. If an owner refuses an interior inspection, the assessor uses the exterior and sales of comparable homes. Owners must be notified whenever an assessment changes.

Appealing an assessment

The path runs through open book and then the Board of Review. Each year the city sets an open book window in Room 308 and a Board of Review date, so ask the Assessor Division for the current schedule. By the time the bill shows up in December it is too late to object, and paying under protest counts only if you first filed with the board.

  • Give notice of intent to object at least 48 hours before the first board meeting, unless you show good cause during the first two hours of that meeting (s. 70.47(7)(a)).
  • File the written objection during those two hours and challenge the combined value of land and improvements.
  • Expect to be sworn in. The assessor has to attend the first meeting.
  • The clerk posts notice at least 15 days ahead, or 30 days in a revaluation year.

After the sale: ownership and forms

The new owner's name reaches the tax bill through the Assessor's Office about two weeks after the deed is recorded with the Register of Deeds. Owner data for bills is normally pulled from the city's database in November, so a house sold between mid-November and December may still show the old owner on that year's bill. Call the Assessor's Office for the latest.

The division also handles a change of address form, available in Room 308, which needs an agent authorization form when someone files for another person. Combining or splitting contiguous parcels you own uses a separate form. Name changes are recorded with the Register of Deeds, where a recorded survey can also be found, at (262) 636-3208, 730 Wisconsin Avenue.

Exemption requests are due at the Assessor's Office by March 1 to count for the current assessment year.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Lottery, homestead and other credits

The lottery and gaming credit shows up as a reduction on a qualifying bill. Apply or remove it through the Department of Revenue's online portal, where late claims are due by October 1. The homestead credit is a different thing, claimed on your Wisconsin income tax return and aimed at lower-income households. The county treasurer explains both, and links a veteran's credit page too.

The Assessor page also links the state's Guide for Property Owners for 2026, which walks through assessment accuracy, tax procedures and yearly valuation updates.

Selling with unpaid taxes

Gather three numbers: current-year installments still owed to the city, any older balance held by the county treasurer, and the interest on both. The title company or closing attorney adds them to the payoff statement. A buyer who takes the house as is still gets a deed that must be recorded with the county, so clean tax records help the closing move.

If you inherited the house, tell the Assessor's Office once the deed is recorded so the bill goes out in the right name. If several years are delinquent, call the county treasurer about the foreclosure timeline before you list. The county sells foreclosed properties by sealed bid and over-the-counter sale, and a sale that closes first avoids that path.

A practical order of calls works well. Start with the Assessor Division in Room 308 to confirm the owner name and parcel details on record. Next phone the city at (262) 636-9171 for what is open for the current year. Then ask the county treasurer about anything older. Last, check with the Register of Deeds at (262) 636-3208 that the deed and any name change were recorded properly. Each office holds a different piece of the file, and a payoff that leaves one out can delay the closing.

Frequently asked questions

Who gets my property tax payment in the City of Racine?

The city, on January 31, March 31, May 31 and July 31. From August 1 on, pay the Racine County Treasurer at 730 Wisconsin Avenue. Payment questions go to (262) 636-9171.

Can I pay in installments in Racine?

Yes. The city offers four, on January 31, March 31, May 31 and July 31. Most other places in Racine County offer two.

When does a new owner appear on a Racine tax bill?

About two weeks after the deed is recorded, the Assessor's Office updates ownership. Names for bills are normally pulled in November, so a mid-November or December sale may not show on that year's bill.

Where is the Racine Assessor's Office?

City Hall, 730 Washington Avenue, Room 308. It handles address changes, parcel splits and combines, and exemption requests, which are due March 1.

When does the Racine Board of Review meet?

The date is set each year. Call the Assessor Division for the open book and board schedule, and give notice 48 hours before the first meeting.

Appleton and its three counties

Appleton is the seat of Outagamie County, on the Fox River about 30 miles southwest of Green Bay. The 2020 census counted 75,644 residents in 24.82 square miles. Most of the city lies in Outagamie County, with smaller pieces in Calumet and Winnebago counties, and the city sits in five school districts. That split affects you in two ways: the Assessor keeps more than one tax rate and assessment level, and delinquent tax goes to a different county treasurer depending on where your parcel falls.

Who assesses and who bills property tax in Appleton?

The city handles both jobs, split between two offices. County involvement begins only after a bill is delinquent.

  • Assessor's Office, (920) 832-5850. Values every parcel, keeps ownership and lot descriptions, and mails a notice when an assessment changes. Revaluation of all property happens at least every five years, and the aim is an inspection of each parcel at least every ten.
  • Finance Department, (920) 832-6442. Bills and collects tax at City Hall, 100 N. Appleton St. On weekdays you can pay at the first-floor desk or the drive-up window, use the night deposit box, mail a check to P.O. Box 2519, Appleton, WI 54912-2519, or pay online through the Payment Center. Paying online adds a processor fee, and none of it goes to the city.
  • City Clerk, (920) 832-6443. Takes notices of intent to object and objection forms for the Board of Review.

The Finance page on the city website carries a copy of your bill and a breakdown of where the money goes. Your tax is the net rate per $1,000 times your assessed value. The rate comes from the combined budgets of the school district, city, county, sewer district, technical college and state reforestation.

Payment dates and delinquent tax

Appleton splits the bill into four installments, due January 31, then March 31, May 31 and July 31, and each date is printed on the statement. State law has bills out by the third Monday in December. If any installment is late, the installment option is cancelled and monthly interest runs from February 1 on the unpaid balance. The interest rate under Wis. Stat. 74.47 is one percent a month, and a county board can tack on up to half a percent monthly as a penalty.

Once a balance is delinquent, the city stops collecting it. The county treasurer takes over unpaid balances from 2025 and earlier, and which county that is depends on the parcel.

Winnebago County1,441(920) 232-3420

Refunds work like this. If you pay in person with an escrow check and are owed $750 or less, you may get the refund in cash. Larger refunds, and any refund on a mailed or drop-box payment, are mailed within four to six weeks. An escrow check payable to the owner and the City of Appleton must be endorsed by both.

How the Appleton assessment and appeal process works

Each spring the city mails a Notice of Changed Assessment, then holds an informal Open Book review ahead of the formal Board of Review. Once the board meets, that year's assessments are final. Ask the Assessor for the calendar for the coming year. The law sets the notice lead time at 15 days before the board meets, stretching to 30 days when the city revalues.

To object, follow the steps the Clerk lists:

  • Start with a conversation with the Assessor, which the Clerk lists as step one.
  • Give the City Clerk notice of intent, spoken or written, no later than 48 hours before the Board of Review first convenes.
  • Hand in Objection Form PA-115A during the first two hours of that first session.
  • Bring evidence. The Board presumes the assessor got it right, so proof is the owner's job.

The board has seven members: the Mayor, the City Clerk, three alderpersons and three residents. A decision can go to circuit court by certiorari within 90 days of the notice of decision under Wis. Stat. 70.47.

By the time the December bill arrives, it is too late to object. Paying under protest is not an objection unless you first appealed to the Board of Review.

Which credits reduce an Appleton tax bill?

The bill can show two state credits. If you lived in the house as your primary residence on January 1 of the levy year, the lottery and gaming credit is yours, and the dollar amount moves from year to year. The first dollar credit is applied automatically to every taxable parcel with an improvement on it, whether or not the owner lives there. For the lottery credit, contact the treasurer of your county.

What you do to the house can also move the assessment. Routine work such as a new furnace, roof repair, gutters or patched walls generally does not raise it, though several items together might. Additions, finished basements, new decks and extensive kitchen or bath remodels usually do. Assessors visit recently sold homes in the fall and winter, so expect a letter after a sale.

What fees apply when I sell an Appleton house?

On a sale, the seller covers the state's 30 cents per $100 of value, a charge written into Wis. Stat. 77.22. Collection happens when the deed is recorded, after both parties sign an electronic transfer return. Whether Outagamie, Calumet or Winnebago County does the recording depends on where the parcel sits.

Wis. Stat. 77.25 exempts certain conveyances from the fee. A deed claiming an exemption has to state its reason right on the document. Examples include transfers by will, descent or survivorship, foreclosure transfers and deeds in lieu to the mortgage holder, sales for delinquent taxes, and transfers between parent and child or grandparent and grandchild for little or no payment. A regular sale to an unrelated buyer does not qualify.

Clearing unpaid Appleton property tax before a sale

Have the title or escrow company order a payoff from the correct treasurer. For the current bill that is the Finance Department. For 2025 and earlier years it is the county treasurer, and the payoff includes interest from February 1. A delinquent real property tax is wiped out by paying the balance, with interest and any penalty, ahead of the date a tax certificate is issued on the parcel.

Do not wait for the bill if a closing will fall near a deadline. Let the closing agent know which installments you have already paid. For an inherited or long-held house with a fuzzy tax history, phone the Finance Department with the parcel number. That call shows quickly what is open.

From listing to closing

The tax side of an Appleton sale follows a short sequence.

  • Find your parcel number and note which county it sits in.
  • Ask Finance at (920) 832-6442 which installments are paid on the current bill.
  • If any earlier year is open, call the county treasurer from the table above for a payoff with interest.
  • Check whether an assessment notice arrived recently, and if you plan to object, remember the Board of Review calendar.
  • Hand the payoff letters to the closing agent, who will settle the balances from your proceeds.

Appleton's three-county layout is the detail most likely to trip up a seller, so write down your county early. A parcel on the Calumet side sends delinquent tax to a different office, and recording happens in that county as well. Sellers in the Winnebago corner, a small slice of the city, should be especially careful because most Appleton guidance assumes Outagamie County.

Selling to a cash buyer can speed things up since no lender is underwriting, though the transfer return, recording and tax payoff are still required.

Frequently asked questions

When are Appleton property taxes due?

Four deadlines: the last day of January, March, May and July. A missed one ends the installment plan and starts interest running from February 1. Payment options are City Hall, mail, the drop box and the online center.

Which county treasurer do I pay if my Appleton taxes are delinquent?

Whichever county treasurer covers the parcel's location: Outagamie at (920) 832-5065, Calumet at (920) 849-1457 or Winnebago at (920) 232-3420. The city sends unpaid balances for 2025 and earlier years there.

How do I appeal my Appleton assessment?

Call the Assessor at (920) 832-5850 first. Next, notify the City Clerk of your intent at least 48 hours before the board's first meeting, and turn in Objection Form PA-115A in that meeting's first two hours.

Seller's transfer fee in Appleton: how does it work?

The seller does. The Register of Deeds takes 30 cents per $100 of value when the deed is recorded. Transfers by inheritance, foreclosure deeds and some family conveyances are exempt.

Can I pay property tax under protest instead of appealing?

No. Paying under protest is not an objection unless you first filed an appeal with the Board of Review. The objection has to happen in spring, before the December bill arrives.
